PHASE PURPOSE: Produce milestones, sequencing, estimates, dependencies, and a risk-managed delivery plan.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Design and build a complex, production-shaped native iOS app that requires a
real server-side backend (not local-only, not a static/offline app) — pick a
genuinely creative, non-obvious idea that solves a real, specific pain point
well enough that it has a real shot at organic/viral growth. Do not default
to another todo-list, habit-tracker, journaling, or AI-wrapper app — those
categories are saturated and none of them are "unique." Think harder for an
underserved, emotionally sticky, inherently-social-or-real-time problem
where a mobile client + backend architecture is actually necessary (real-time
sync across users/devices, a shared/live data feed, matching or coordination
between people, server-side processing too heavy for on-device, etc.) — the
backend requirement should come from the idea being genuinely multi-user or
real-time, not be bolted on.

Requirements for the idea itself (spend real effort on this — the idea is
the deliverable, not just the code):
- Solves one specific, sharply-defined pain point for a specific audience
  (not "everyone"). Be able to state the pain point and audience in one
  sentence each.
- Has a natural viral/sharing loop baked into the core mechanic — not a
  bolted-on "invite friends" button, but something where using the app is
  inherently more valuable or fun with other people, or naturally produces
  something worth sharing outside the app.
- Genuinely requires a backend: real-time multiplayer/sync, a live shared
  feed, server-side matching/aggregation, push notifications driven by
  server-side events, or similar — justify the architecture choice.
- Is creative enough that a stranger hearing the one-line pitch would say
  "oh that's clever" rather than "isn't that just [existing app]?"

Technical scope:
- Native iOS client (SwiftUI).
- A real backend service (your choice of stack — pick something sensible
  and justify it) handling auth, data sync/storage, and whatever real-time
  or server-side logic the concept needs.
- Design the API contract, data model, and sync/real-time strategy properly
  before building — this is a "complicated app," not an MVP toy.
- Production-shaped: reasonable auth flow, error handling, loading/empty/
  offline states, and a coherent onboarding funnel a real user could follow.
- Visual design should be distinctive and match the concept — not generic
  default SwiftUI styling — but the primary bar for this app is the idea,
  the architecture, and it actually working end-to-end (client <-> backend).

Start by proposing and committing to the specific concept (pain point,
audience, viral loop, and why it needs a backend) before moving into specs
and build, and carry that concept consistently through naming, design, and
onboarding copy.

## Final Output

This phase confirms: **single-app build, no portfolio split.** The prompt asked for one native iOS app, and the concept that emerged from prompt_contract and product_research — a trust-graph-restricted, real-time pickup-relay coordination app for a school pickup pod — is inherently one app, not a decomposable set of sibling apps.

Selected app:
- **slug:** `pulse-relay`
- **category:** real-time trust-graph coordination / social-utility (explicitly not marketplace, not generic messaging, not "matching")
- **promise:** When a parent can't make pickup, their pod knows within seconds and exactly one person locks it in — no double coverage, no guessing who saw the message.
- **target user:** A parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod (one classroom/carpool cluster) hit by an unplanned same-day pickup conflict.
- **build:** true

Rejected alternatives: splitting into sibling apps (separate requester/helper apps, a pod-admin companion app, a group-chat clone, a caregiver marketplace, a generic emergency-alert app); generic todo/habit/journal/AI-wrapper reskins; single-user-only designs; open stranger/proximity matching; daycare/activity pod variants in v1; location-tracking-first designs. `portfolio_json` is null — this is not a portfolio parent.

Build-priority guidance carried into later phases: if build time is constrained, cut breadth in secondary screens (pod management, profile/settings polish) before ever compromising the correctness or speed of the two locked core funnels (post relay request → pod visibility; accept → conflict-resolve → complete), since the core loop's trustworthiness is the entire value proposition.

{"phase": "initial_discussion", "one_paragraph_summary": "The initial_discussion phase locked a single, mutually-confirmed product definition for pulse-relay across two rounds. Product promise: a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcasts a same-day pickup coverage need and exactly one trusted pod member locks it in via a server-arbitrated first-accept-wins mechanism, with no ambiguity and no silent failure states. Primary user: a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod, acting one-handed under real time pressure with roughly ninety seconds of attention. The core loop was locked with explicit named states end-to-end: post request (no child PII) -> live pod visibility + push deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional time-aware still-open escalation with re-broadcast -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record.   rationale: The receipt card can only fire after a successful completion, so it is a lagging artifact of things already having gone right, not a mechanism that makes things go right; over-investing build time in the card's polish while core-loop reliability has rough edges would misallocate effort against what actually drives pod-level adoption.
  rejected: Treating the shareable receipt card as the primary viral growth feature; Building a dedicated invite/referral screen as the growth mechanic
  constraints: No later phase may introduce an 'invite your pod' or referral screen framed as the primary growth mechanic; First-incident reliability (notification latency, race-condition correctness) must be prioritized in build order ahead of receipt-card visual polish
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] No optimistic UI confirmation is permitted anywhere in the client for outcome-affecting actions (accept, release, complete); an explicit 'sending / awaiting confirmation' transitional state must appear between user tap and server acknowledgment, even for a fraction of a second.

  constraints: This is a hard constraint on the API contract and client state machine in the next (architecture) phase, not a polish item
- [DEC-next_steps_small-001] The MVP slice for pulse-relay is the entire core loop end-to-end (post, live visibility + push, accept-race arbitration, release/reopen, still-open escalation, complete, audit/receipt) run by two real seeded accounts in one pod — not a stripped-down subset of it.
  rationale: The app has no secondary value proposition to fall back on; a subset that omits race arbitration, release, or still-open escalation is a different, less defensible app that happens to share a name, not a smaller version of pulse-relay.
  rejected: A smaller slice covering only post-and-accept without race arbitration, release, or still-open escalation; Treating this slice as a screen-by-screen build target rather than one complete incident workflow
  constraints: Later build phases must implement this slice as one continuous workflow tested with two real accounts, not as isolated screens
- [DEC-next_steps_small-002] The accept-race 'already covered by [name]' loser transition is locked as critical-path, non-negotiable-quality UX within this MVP slice, prioritized above other visual work in the slice including the shareable receipt card — it is explicitly carved out of the 'polish-only UI' cut bucket.

  rejected: Treating the loser-state transition as an equal-priority correctness item alongside all other MVP screens, with visual treatment decided later as generic polish; Bundling this transition into the same cut-list tier as animations, theming, and iconography
  constraints: The next design phase must name this transition explicitly and not lump it into generic 'polish' decisions; Build priority within this slice puts this transition's fidelity ahead of receipt-card visual investment
- [DEC-next_steps_small-003] This MVP slice must use real server-side compare-and-swap arbitration and real APNs-delivered push notifications for the accept-race outcome; polling or client-side arbitration is explicitly disallowed as a stand-in, even if it would satisfy the same UI-state acceptance checklist.

- [DEC-next_steps_small-004] The acceptance bar for this slice is a literal two-phone side-by-side demo — two real seeded accounts on two real devices where one confirms and the other shows 'already covered by [name]' within a second or two, with zero chat and zero manual reconciliation — with all itemized validation criteria (backend reachability, race-test determinism, push timing, release/reopen timing, still-open aging, force-quit persistence) serving as constituent checks within that demo rather than a separate competing checklist.

  rejected: Treating the itemized validation criteria as a flat checklist with no single unifying acceptance demo
  constraints: Verification in the build phase should be run and judged as this literal two-device demo, with the itemized criteria checked as part of it
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The client shows honest, literal delivery-count copy on post ('Sent to N pod members') based on actual push registration/token status, with a warning banner if delivery looks uncertain, rather than implying full pod visibility.
  rationale: The free tier has no critical-alert/DND-bypass, so silent notification failure on a new pod's first incident is a real and likely failure mode; pretending otherwise would recreate the false-confidence problem this app exists to eliminate.
  rejected: Generic 'notification sent' copy that implies everyone was reached; Treating notification reliability as solvable in v1 and deferring the copy decision
  constraints: This must be documented as an accepted free-tier limitation, not treated as a bug to be silently patched later
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Same-day cutoffs and elapsed-time/aging calculations are computed entirely server-side using UTC timestamps plus a pod-home-timezone value set once at pod creation; no client-local-time logic is used for these calculations.
  rationale: Per-device local time creates ambiguous same-day boundaries and inconsistent aging displays across devices/timezones, undermining the 'no ambiguity, ever' requirement, especially for co-parenting pods with members in different timezones.
  rejected: Using device-local time to determine same-day cutoffs or elapsed time
  constraints: Pod home timezone must be captured at pod creation and used as the sole reference for date/aging math
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw) carries a client-generated idempotent action ID; the server must handle duplicate submissions idempotently, and any relaunch after a force-quit/crash must reconcile from server truth rather than trusting stale local UI state. A force-quit-mid-accept-before-ack scenario is a named acceptance test alongside the two-phone race demo.
  rationale: Without idempotency, retries or crash-relaunches during outcome-affecting actions could create duplicate requests or leave a device showing an outcome that never actually happened server-side, directly violating the no-false-confirmation principle.
  rejected: Leaving crash/retry behavior as an implementation detail discovered during build or QA
  constraints: This is a hard requirement on the API contract and client state machine in the architecture phase, not a polish item; The force-quit-mid-accept test case must be run and verified, not just described
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The pod-creator role gains exactly one additional capability beyond create-pod-and-get-code: revoke-and-reissue the join code, invalidating the old code immediately on rotation.

  rejected: Leaving join codes permanent and un-revocable; Building a full pod-admin console with member management to address this
  constraints: No other admin/moderation capability is added alongside this one
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] A pod with no members other than its creator gets a distinct empty state and CTA ('share the invite') that is visually and semantically separate from 'pod has other members but nobody has responded yet' (re-broadcast/escalate CTA).
  rationale: Collapsing these two very different situations into one generic 'waiting' state would recreate the false-confidence failure mode this app is built to eliminate, since a solo pod and an unresponsive pod require completely different next actions from the user.
  rejected: A single generic waiting/pending empty state covering both situations
  constraints: Design and build phases must treat these as two distinct, named UI states, not variants of the same screen
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The audit/receipt record persists after either party deletes their account, with the departed party rendered as a placeholder (e.g. 'Former member') in both the internal audit view and the shareable projection.
  rationale: The record may serve as custody/co-parenting documentation for the other party; allowing either party to unilaterally erase it via account deletion would undermine the entire evidence model the export feature was built to serve.
  rejected: Cascading deletion of the audit/receipt record when either party deletes their account
  constraints: Account deletion logic must explicitly exclude audit/receipt records from cascading deletes
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] UI copy and help text must explicitly state that an 'accepted' request means a trusted pod member has claimed responsibility, never that help or on-time arrival is guaranteed.
  rationale: Without this, users could reasonably infer a stronger guarantee than the app actually provides, especially since v1 has no location/ETA tracking to verify actual arrival.
  rejected: Leaving this distinction implicit and undocumented
  constraints: This must appear as visible copy on the accepted/claimed state, not just be an internal design assumption
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Add a first-class, requester-only terminal `withdrawn` state for same-day requests, usable only while the request is still open/still-open/reopened and unclaimed; it is arbitrated through the same server-side CAS mechanism as accept (so a race between an incoming accept and a withdraw resolves deterministically), triggers a real push/re-notify to the pod, and never generates an audit/receipt artifact. It is visually and semantically distinct from `complete` (e.g. muted/gray 'Withdrawn — no longer needed', not the green completion/receipt state).
  rationale: Without an explicit withdraw path, a self-resolved situation leaves a stale, actively-escalating open request that can lead a good-faith pod member to accept and act on a need that no longer exists — a real-world harm on par with the false-positive-confirmation risk the rest of the state machine is designed to prevent. Auto-closure alone doesn't cover the acute window before expiry kicks in.
  rejected: Relying solely on bounded auto-closure plus manual re-post, with no requester-facing withdraw action; Treating stale-request cleanup as a passive warning rather than an explicit requester-triggered state; Allowing a generic 'cancel' to behave like or be visually similar to a completed handoff
  constraints: `withdrawn` must never generate an audit/receipt artifact, since no handoff occurred; `withdrawn` must use a CAS-arbitrated write and idempotent action IDs like every other outcome-affecting action; `withdrawn` must be visually and copy-wise distinct from `complete` and `error` at the same fidelity bar as the 'already covered' transition
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The `withdrawn` and `release` actions are mutually exclusive by state: withdraw is only ever visible to the requester while the request is open/still-open (unclaimed); once a request is accepted, only the accepter's `release` action is available and withdraw disappears entirely.
  rationale: This eliminates the specific ambiguity risk that motivated hesitation about adding a cancel-like action — a user is never shown an action that could be misread as undoing someone else's commitment, because the two actions never coexist for the same request.
  rejected: Allowing withdraw to remain visible or available after a request has been accepted
  constraints: Client and server logic must enforce this mutual exclusivity as a state-machine invariant, not just a UI convention
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] V1 ships with no in-app moderation, reporting, muting, or member-removal capability to handle bad-faith or spam posting by a known pod member; this is an explicit, named, accepted limitation, mitigated only by trust-graph invite-only membership, per-request attribution/auditability, and the creator's code revoke/reissue capability.
  rationale: Building real moderation would reopen the admin-console/member-management scope deliberately cut in earlier phases for good reasons; leaving the risk undocumented would be worse than naming it plainly, consistent with how cold-start and Focus/DND limitations were handled.
  rejected: Adding member removal, reporting, or rate-limiting capability in v1; Leaving this risk unaddressed and undocumented
  constraints: Onboarding/help copy must state plainly that this is a trust-graph, invitation-based tool for known pods, not a moderated public platform; This limitation cannot be used to justify degrading any core-loop guarantee (APNs delivery, receipt integrity, state-machine correctness, four-state screens)
- [DEC-app_features-001] Must-have features are split into execution-priority tiers for build scheduling only: Tier-1 (auth persistence, zero-state create-or-join onboarding, no-PII posting with awaiting-confirmation, honest delivery-count copy, server-committed push dispatch, and CAS-based accept-race determinism) forms the literal two-phone demo and cannot be rushed; Tier-2 (release/reopen, withdrawn, still-open aging/re-broadcast, completion-to-receipt) remains fully required but may ship with rougher visual polish first if time is short.
  rationale: Both participants agreed the app has no fallback value proposition if the demo-critical race/notification path is wrong, so any time pressure must be absorbed by the less catastrophic parts of the loop, never the part that proves the backend is load-bearing.
  rejected: Treating all must-have features as equally weighted with no execution order; Making release/withdraw/still-open lower-priority in a way that could drop their correctness, not just their polish
  constraints: Tier-2 items remain required outcomes in the graded contract, not optional; Only visual/UX polish may be reduced under time pressure, never state-machine or server-invariant correctness
- [DEC-app_features-002] Subscription-tier features (multi-pod membership, exportable/signed receipt history, critical-alert notification bypass) are explicitly out of implementation scope for this build: no StoreKit integration, no paywall UI, no core behavior gated behind entitlement.
  rationale: Building paid-tier scaffolding does not increase confidence that the core trust-graph relay works under real concurrent pressure, and would divert time from the one thing this build must prove — real backend-load-bearing, two-device race correctness.
  rejected: Implementing paywall/subscription screens or entitlement checks in this build; Treating the three unlocks as hidden must-have build tasks
  constraints: Any schema entitlement fields must remain inert and unused in this build; No UI may reference or imply an unavailable premium flow
- [DEC-app_features-003] Tiering is strictly a scheduling/finish-quality mechanism, not a requirements-erosion mechanism: every must-have requirement remains required for acceptance, and all core invariants (CAS arbitration, idempotency, withdraw/release state exclusivity, four-state visibility, server-owned time semantics, no-optimistic terminal confirmation) must be implemented and testable regardless of tier.
  rationale: Prevents a build agent from reading the tiering as license to ship an incomplete or UI-only version of a 'lower tier' state transition under time pressure.
  rejected: Allowing partial or cosmetic-only implementations of core invariants for Tier-2 items when time is short
  constraints: A build that preserves UI layout for a Tier-2 screen but drops or fakes its underlying state transition is non-compliant, regardless of tier
- [DEC-app_features-004] The tokenized Theme.swift system and full light/dark coverage on every core screen is locked as a hard must-have with design-lint parity — no hardcoded font, size, spacing, or color literal outside the theme file, and no core-screen visual sign-off without both appearances verified.
  rationale: This fleet already has two recorded design-lint incidents matching exactly this failure (hardcoded font size, hardcoded inline color), and the global phase playbook already requires tokenized styling and dark-mode as a hard rule, not a stylistic nicety; leaving it on a 'should' list risked a build agent treating it as optional after spending its budget on core-loop correctness.
  rejected: Keeping the tokenized theme system on the should/could list; Allowing inline style literals in feature views with cleanup deferred; Treating dark-mode support as a later polish pass
  constraints: All core screens must reference Theme.swift for typography/color/spacing; Any screen with non-theme-sourced style literals is out of scope for acceptance
- [DEC-app_features-005] R-006, R-007, R-009, R-010, R-011, and R-037 are explicitly labeled demo-critical/uncuttable within the requirements contract itself: honest delivery-count copy, the server-side CAS/arbitration path, the deterministic winner/loser split, non-optimistic terminal confirmation, the bounded server-side push-dispatch commitment, and the literal two-device side-by-side demo.
  rationale: Under real schedule pressure a build agent can misjudge which corner is safe to cut; naming the safety-proof requirements explicitly in the document removes that judgment call rather than relying on inferred tiering alone.
  rejected: Relying on Tier-1/Tier-2 labeling alone to protect the safety-critical subset; Allowing any demo-critical requirement to be downgraded or softened under time pressure
  constraints: If any demo-critical requirement is incomplete, the build is non-compliant regardless of progress on Tier-2 items; Architecture and state-machine docs in later phases must carry these six requirements forward as explicitly non-negotiable
- [DEC-app_features-006] R-007 (push delivery) is locked as a two-part contract: the backend must commit the CAS write and submit the APNs payload within a strict server-owned bound (target <=2s happy-path), while actual device receipt timing is an empirically-observed property of the two-device demo, not a hard API-level pass/fail metric, given Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort.
  rationale: Prevents the requirements document from making an impossible-to-guarantee promise about third-party infrastructure while still holding the backend to strict, verifiable, server-side latency discipline.
  rejected: Wording the requirement as guaranteed/immediate end-to-end device delivery; Treating any observed APNs delay during the demo as an automatic backend defect
  constraints: Backend should target and log server-side dispatch timing as verifiable telemetry; Demo observations of infra-side delay are noted as delivery-UX risk, not treated as a false-positive architecture failure
- [DEC-design_discussion-001] The card status palette is locked as amber-pulse for open/awaiting/live requests, warm teal-green (not stoplight green) for confirmed/claimed, slate/muted gray for terminal non-actionable states (withdrawn, complete), with true red reserved exclusively for genuine system/network errors — never used for any normal product state including the accept-race loser.
  rationale: A parent glancing at this screen mid-panic reads color before text; using alarm-register colors (stoplight red/green, sci-fi HUD blue) for normal outcomes would misrepresent the emotional register the whole product promise depends on (relief, not alarm), and would risk the uncuttable already-covered transition reading as a malfunction.
  rejected: Literal stoplight red/green state coding; Cold blue-black sci-fi/military HUD palette with electric accents
  constraints: Theme.swift must define these as semantic color roles, not literals scattered through views; Red may never be used to render 'already covered by [name]' or any other non-error terminal state
- [DEC-design_discussion-002] The signature interaction is a pulse-to-latch motion: an open request card pulses on a calm heartbeat rhythm while awaiting server acknowledgment, then converts to a steady locked-panel state on resolution. Both the accept-race winner ('claimed/confirmed') and loser ('already covered by [name]') receive this same fast, mechanical, half-second latch treatment — no shake, no alert icon, no error styling on the loser.
  rationale: The losing side of the accept-race is the one moment in the product where 'you didn't get what you tapped for' is the correct, designed outcome (already flagged demo-critical/uncuttable in app_features); giving it the identical calm-latch treatment as the winner is what makes the two-phone demo read as 'the app worked' rather than 'the app broke' at a glance, without requiring the viewer to read any text.
  rejected: A plain status-chip text swap with no accompanying motion; Distinct/error-styled treatment for the losing transition (shake, alert icon, red accent)
  constraints: Reduce Motion must collapse the pulse/latch to an instant but still visually distinct crossfade, not remove the state distinction entirely; This transition's fidelity takes priority over all other visual polish in the build, per the earlier locked build-priority decisions
- [DEC-design_discussion-003] Default SwiftUI chrome is explicitly rejected: no plain List/Form rows, no default NavigationStack system-blue accents, and no transient toast-style confirmation (e.g. a flashing 'Accepted!' that disappears) for any outcome-affecting action.
  rationale: A row-list reads as an inbox and a vanishing toast is exactly the kind of easy-to-miss confirmation this app exists to eliminate; both would recreate the ambiguous-group-chat mental model the product is built to replace.
  rejected: Standard List/Form-based request feed with system accent color; Toast/alert-based confirmation for accept/release/complete/withdraw
  constraints: All outcome-affecting states must be persistent, baked into the card itself, sourced only from real backend acknowledgment
- [DEC-design_discussion-004] Screen scope stays deliberately narrow: session/auth gate, pod onboarding (create or join with true empty states), the live relay board, request composer, request detail (accept/release/withdraw), receipt, and minimal profile/pod-settings — no additional branching or surface area.
  rationale: Matches the build-priority guidance locked in portfolio_selection and app_features: this phase's entire purpose is eliminating claim/no-claim ambiguity, and any added screens or navigation branches would compete with that fidelity for build time.
  rejected: Adding richer navigation, tabs, or additional secondary screens at this stage
  constraints: Any future screen proposal must justify itself against directly reducing false-certainty or missed-coverage risk in the core loop
- [DEC-design_discussion-005] The design language's final name is 'Relay HUD.' The pulse-to-latch motion is the signature interaction within it, not a second brand name, and should be reflected in code as a concrete component name (e.g. BeaconCard/RelayBeaconView).
  rationale: A shorter, single name is what actually gets used in docs, code, and UI copy dozens of times through the build; 'Beacon' surviving as the literal name of the reusable motion component gives build agents a greppable identifier instead of a second competing brand term.
  rejected: 'Relay Beacon HUD' as the full product design-language name; Two parallel names (HUD for structure, Beacon for motion) with no clear precedence
  constraints: Design docs, Theme file comments, and onboarding copy should refer to the language as Relay HUD; The pulse-to-latch component should carry 'Beacon' in its SwiftUI type name
- [DEC-design_discussion-006] Secondary screens (receipt, profile/sign-out, pod settings/code rotation) inherit Theme tokens, spacing, typography, and state language but are explicitly barred from: custom entrance/exit transitions beyond the system default, bespoke empty-state illustration work (a plain SF Symbol plus one line of Theme-styled text is the ceiling), and any color treatment outside the shared semantic palette. The receipt card is a narrow exception only in that it gets a higher bar for typography and information hierarchy (since it leaves the app via the share sheet), but still receives no second signature animation.
  rationale: Turning 'utility-only' into named, specific bans prevents a build agent with spare time from investing craft budget into a secondary screen's own micro-interaction, which would come directly at the expense of the accept-race card's fidelity — the one thing this app is actually judged on.
  rejected: Leaving secondary-screen restraint as a soft 'keep it small' instruction with no named boundaries; Allowing the receipt card its own signature motion given its external-facing role
  constraints: Any secondary-screen work proposing custom motion or bespoke illustration is out of scope for this build; The receipt card's added craft budget is limited to typography/layout quality, not animation
- [DEC-design_discussion-007] The live board's default 'all clear' resting state — no open requests, quiet pod — is a real, composed screen: pod name, member count, an at-rest (non-pulsing) 'all clear' indicator using the same slate/teal semantic language, and the post-request CTA as the single obvious action. It does not get its own unique signature motion, but it must not be a blank view or a bare icon-plus-button placeholder.

  rejected: Treating the resting state as a trivial placeholder screen since all design energy goes to the high-stress states; Giving the resting state its own signature motion, which would violate the secondary/non-critical-screen austerity principle
  constraints: The resting state must use the same Theme tokens and semantic palette as the active board, at rest rather than pulsing; This screen is exempt from the 'zero unique motion' secondary-screen rule only in that it needs real composed content, not in that it needs its own animation
- [DEC-design_discussion-008] If build time is constrained, visual/motion craft budget is spent in this strict order: (1) the open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) the deterministic winner/loser latch resolution, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — with everything else (secondary screens, resting state) built plain and correct rather than polished.
  rationale: Names an explicit tiebreak so a build agent under deadline pressure doesn't have to guess where to cut visual finish, directly extending the Tier-1/Tier-2 execution-priority logic already locked in app_features into concrete design-craft terms.
  rejected: Leaving craft-budget prioritization implicit and inferred from the rest of this phase's output
  constraints: No craft time should go to secondary-screen polish before all three named priorities are fully realized
- [DEC-design_handoff-001] Codex's structured DESIGN SPEC (type scale, spacing grid, component inventory, navigation map, motion/haptics, accessibility) is adopted as the canonical base for this phase, extended with Claude's client-state-machine layer rather than replaced by a competing token set.

  constraints: Any further palette changes must be surgical edits to Codex's existing token file, not a wholesale replacement
- [DEC-design_handoff-002] The request/card state machine distinguishes awaitingConfirmation (this device's own action in flight) from reconciling (state learned via a push-triggered refetch) as separate internal states sharing the pulse visual, plus queuedOffline (action taken with no connection, not yet in flight) and a distinct 'no longer open' state for a deep-link that resolves to a withdrawn/expired request — all four folded into the formal per-screen spec, not left as an inferred edge case.

  rejected: Treating reconciling as the same internal case as awaitingConfirmation; Rendering a queued offline action as a generic awaiting-confirmation spinner; Rendering an expired/withdrawn deep-link target as a generic error state
  constraints: Build must implement all four as named, distinct internal states, not just visually similar variants of two states
- [DEC-design_handoff-003] Screen graph and navigation are locked: AppGate resolves to AuthGate, PodOnboarding, or RelayBoard (default root); RelayBoard presents RequestComposer and RequestDetail as sheets, with RequestDetail also serving as the push deep-link destination; Profile and PodSettings are reachable only via stack push from the board header. No tabs, no additional navigation branches.
  rationale: Matches the narrow-screen-scope discipline already locked in design_discussion and keeps the IA aligned with the app's actual single-core-loop workload rather than adding chrome for an app with essentially one screen that matters.
  rejected: A tab-based root; Additional top-level navigation branches beyond the core loop and two secondary screens
  constraints: No later phase may add tabs or additional root-level navigation destinations
- [DEC-design_handoff-004] Motion timing is locked: the open-to-awaiting pulse is a 0.9s ease-in-out repeating breathing animation (scale 0.99→1.02 plus border alpha oscillation); resolution to either winner or loser uses an identical 0.45s mechanical spring latch (response 0.45, damping 0.82); Reduce Motion collapses both to a ~0.15s crossfade that preserves the text/icon state change; haptics never differentiate winner from loser as success versus warning/error.

  rejected: Distinct or error-styled haptic/motion treatment for the losing transition
  constraints: No implementation may give the loser transition a different duration, curve, or haptic category than the winner
- [DEC-design_handoff-005] If build time is constrained, visual/motion craft effort is spent in this order: (1) the open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) the winner/loser latch resolution, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — before any polish on the board resting state or secondary screens.
  rationale: Directly carries forward the craft-budget tiebreak already locked in design_discussion into this phase's concrete spec, so a build agent under deadline pressure has an explicit order rather than having to infer one.
  rejected: Leaving craft-budget priority unstated in this phase's own spec and relying solely on the prior phase's mention of it
  constraints: No craft time goes to secondary-screen or resting-state polish before all three named priorities are fully realized
- [DEC-design_handoff-007] The Relay HUD surface/neutral system is corrected to a warm-neutral palette (warm off-white backgrounds, warm charcoal dark surfaces) replacing the cool-blue scaffold from the earlier draft, while all state accent colors (amber pulse, teal confirmed, slate terminal, error red) remain unchanged.
  rationale: The neutral scaffolding, not the state accents, was the remaining source of the 'cold blue-black sci-fi HUD' register explicitly rejected in design_discussion's DEC-design_discussion-001; a cold base can trigger an alarm register even when state accents are correct.
  rejected: Keeping the blue-leaning neutral tokens on the grounds that state accents were already correct; Claude's independently-proposed alternate warm hex values, treated as confirming the same fix rather than a competing spec since both point the same direction
  constraints: All base surface/divider/background/card tones in Theme.swift must use the warm-neutral values in the final palette table; No non-tokenized neutral literals anywhere outside Theme.swift
- [DEC-design_handoff-008] Relay board request ordering is exclusively server-authoritative displayOrder (created-at ascending plus a deterministic backend tie-break); no client-side urgency computation or local re-sort exists anywhere in the spec.

### Round 3


**Codex (Red Team · Closer) — Round 3**

I’m locking this round down hard because leaving this unresolved just means one of you hits the wrong type names in code and the other hits the wrong API body at runtime. Codex and Claude both got the same behavior, but the nouns drifted; I’m choosing a single canonical naming/shape set now and we can stop second-guessing it.

Decision 1: the canonical domain model family is `Request`-based, not `PulseRequest`/`RelayRequest`. So it is `Request`, `RequestAction`, `RequestReceipt`, `RequestStatus`, etc. This keeps types concise, aligns with Apple naming ergonomics, and reduces cognitive load in both client and backend workers. I’ll call out `Request` as the shared term across UI, coordinator, API, and storage.

Decision 2: expired requests stay a close-reason concern, not a new request status value. `RequestStatus` stays at five values: `open`, `claimed`, `reopened`, `withdrawn`, `completed`. `Request` gets `closeReason: RequestCloseReason?` with at least `autoExpired`, `requesterWithdrawn`, `systemHousekeeping`. This preserves actionability invariants (state machine transitions remain small) while still giving deterministic copy for "expired/no-longer-open" branches, and avoids a pseudo-12th terminal state in the client card machine.

Decision 3: `ActionType` must include `reBroadcast` (again). This is not optional. DEC-initial requirement says escalation/re-broadcast for still-open is part of the core loop and the two-phone demo correctness bar still depends on it. It also gives us an explicit intent signal for "nudge the pod again" without abusing release/withdraw semantics.

Decision 4: `expectedRequestRevision` is required for all action mutations from the client to server and from coordinator to wire. `POST /requests/{id}/actions` receives non-optional `expectedRequestRevision: UInt64`; coordinator methods pass it through as required. This is the only way we avoid replay ambiguity on queued/offline reconciliation and make stale-write rejection deterministic. `postRequest` and `fetch` remain independent.

Decision 5: we add a third mandatory verification path: backend integration concurrency (already required), plus local coordinator concurrency, plus the side-by-side demo. The new local-path check is specifically for actor correctness under real contention: two `RequestSyncCoordinator` instances (simulating two devices) issue accept concurrently against a shared test backend, then assert each sees the same winner/loser outcome through their event stream. This catches reducer/queue/refetch race bugs that pure HTTP tests can miss, then still runs before the two-phone manual demo.

I’m also adding one red-team gap that was missing: queued actions with conflict responses must not spin forever. Scenario: user taps Accept while on a bad connection; action goes `queuedOffline` with revision, then reconnects after multiple conflicting retries; backend now returns `staleData`/`alreadyClaimed`. If we keep requeueing blindly, the UI can sit in limbo and violate the “no false confidence” rule. Coordinator must classify conflict/forbidden/unauthorized outcomes as terminal for that action (move to explicit error/reveal branch and stop retries), while only network/timeout errors are retriable. This should be explicit in reducer and test coverage.

Architecture-wise, we stay on the spine already locked: SwiftData cache + durable outbox, actor coordinator, enum-based request phases, server-order authority, and push as wake-up only. File/module layout for build lanes: `App/` (`PulseRelayApp.swift`, `AppSession.swift`, `AppGate.swift`), `Domain/` (all models/events/reducer), `State/` (`RequestSyncCoordinator`, reducer tests), `Network/` (`RequestAPIClient`, URLSession endpoints/mappers), `Persistence/` (`SwiftData` models + cache reset + recovery), `Notifications/` (`PushService`, deep-link parsing), `Features/` (`AuthGate`, `PodOnboarding`, `RelayBoard`, `RequestComposer`, `RequestDetail`, `Receipt`, `Profile`, `PodSettings`), `Shared/` (Theme, timers/formatters/haptics/accessibility helpers). This is small enough for one build lane and hard to fork.

Persistence strategy remains: `RequestSnapshot`/`PodSnapshot` cache is disposable and purge/refetch-on-schema-mismatch; `OutboxAction` is durable across relaunch/upgrade and explicitly preserved across cache resets. `KeychainStore` uses `AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` and no business data is considered source-of-truth. We keep only one place of truth in memory for request phase transitions: the reducer fed by coordinator events.

Testing strategy: Swift Testing for reducer state transitions (including queued/awaiting/reconciling separation, close-reason rendering, stale conflict handling), DTO/coding round-trips, and elapsed-time formatting against serverNow. Backend concurrent tests for accept-vs-accept and accept-vs-withdraw with deterministic conflict assertions remain mandatory. Add local coordinator race test using TaskGroup on two actor instances; then run the manual two-device side-by-side acceptance demo as final behavioral proof.

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Visionary) — Round 3**

Okay, let's actually close this instead of doing another lap. The coordinator called out that Codex and I swapped naming preferences mid-air without seeing each other's swap, which is a genuinely funny failure mode but an easy one to fix once someone just looks at the actual reasoning instead of the position. Codex, you wrote "your naming is cleaner than the RelayRequest/ActionRecord split for compile stability" — and I think that reasoning is just correct on its own merits, independent of who said it first. `Request` doesn't actually collide with anything in Foundation (no bare `Request` type exists there), we own the whole namespace, and a `Relay` prefix on every single domain noun starts reading like Hungarian notation by the third or fourth type. I'm dropping my round-2 `Relay*` push and going with the plain family: `Request`, `RequestStatus`, `RequestAction`, `ActionType`, `ActionResult`, `Receipt`, `Pod`, `PodMembership`, `User`. No more ping-pong on this — picking it and moving on.

On expired-vs-withdrawn, I want to actually change my mind here, not just split the difference. I proposed expanding `RequestStatus` to six values; you proposed keeping status at five and adding a separate `RequestCloseReason` field with `autoExpired` / `requesterWithdrawn` / `systemHousekeeping`. Sitting with both for a second, yours is the better design, and not just because it's already written — it's a cleaner separation of concerns. `status` answers "what state is this row in," `closeReason` answers "why did it get here," and that split gives us room for a category (`systemHousekeeping`) we haven't even needed yet but might, without ever touching the status enum again. My version conflated those two questions into one field, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine now and gets awkward the first time we need a second system-driven reason that isn't expiry. So: `RequestStatus` stays at `open, claimed, reopened, withdrawn, completed`, and `closeReason: RequestCloseReason?` carries the why for withdrawn rows. The client's `.withdrawn(Request)` card phase reads `request.closeReason` to pick copy — same visual, same lack of a receipt CTA, different string. I'm taking your version outright.

`reBroadcast` stays in `ActionType` — you didn't object to it, you just hadn't seen my round-2 message when you wrote yours, and the requirement backing it (DEC-initial_discussion-005, "a re-broadcast path" on a still-open request) isn't something either of us has any actual grounds to cut. I'm locking it as a sixth action type with the CAS guard `allowed_from = [open, reopened]`, requester-only, unless you come back and specifically say you want it out — but there's no requirements-based reason to, so I don't expect that.

On `expectedRequestRevision`, you made it required and I had it optional at the `performAction`/coordinator layer, and thinking about it again, required is just correct and I was being sloppily defensive for no reason. There's no legitimate call site where the coordinator invokes `perform(requestId:action:expectedRequestRevision:)` without already knowing the last-known revision — it always has a cached `Request` in hand before it can even show the accept/release/withdraw button in the first place, so making the parameter optional just opens a hole where some future call site accidentally passes `nil` and silently defeats the whole guard your round-one scenario was built around. Required, non-optional `UInt64`, full stop. The one place it stays optional is inside `OutboxAction` itself, and only because that same model also stores queued `post` actions, which create a new request and have no prior revision to guard against — so the field is `UInt64?` at the storage layer but effectively required by construction for every action type except `post`.

Last thing — nobody's pushed back on the two-coordinator concurrent test tier I proposed last round, so I'm treating it as landed: two real `RequestSyncCoordinator` instances in one test process, each with a distinct fake identity, both wired to one local test-backend instance, racing an `accept` inside a `TaskGroup`, asserting the winner's stream emits `latchedConfirmed` and the loser's emits `latchedAlreadyCovered` with the correct name populated. That sits between Codex's backend-only HTTP concurrency test and the physical two-phone demo, and it's the only tier that actually exercises the reducer and the coordinator against real concurrent network timing without needing two devices in a room every time someone touches this code.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 3**

Three rounds in, and this one actually lands. Codex made the call everyone had been dancing around — plain `Request`-family naming, no `Relay` prefix — and instead of relitigating it, Claude looked at her own reasoning from last round, agreed it was right independent of who said it first, and dropped her own push for the opposite. Same thing happened on the expired-vs-withdrawn question: Claude explicitly said "I want to change my mind here, not just split the difference" and took Codex's separate `closeReason` field over her own status-enum expansion, giving a real reason (status answers "what state," closeReason answers "why," and conflating them would've gotten awkward the first time a second system-driven reason showed up). `reBroadcast` is back in both drafts with identical semantics. `expectedRequestRevision` is now required, non-optional, on both sides — Claude walked back her own "optional" stance, saying it was "sloppily defensive for no reason" since the coordinator never invokes accept/release/withdraw without already holding a cached request revision in hand. And the new coordinator-level concurrent test tier Claude proposed last round with no response is now explicitly locked by Codex as "Decision 5," non-negotiable, alongside the backend HTTP test and the physical two-phone demo.

Codex also did the one thing this phase's rules actually require of the Red Team seat and hadn't landed yet: a genuinely new edge case — a queued offline action that comes back from the server with a real conflict (already claimed, no longer open) must not just sit there retrying forever, because that would quietly recreate the exact false-confidence failure this whole app exists to prevent. Conflict/forbidden/unauthorized outcomes are terminal for that action; only network/timeout failures get retried. Claude didn't respond to this one directly, but it doesn't clash with anything she locked, it's a straightforward consequence of the reducer/terminal-state discipline both of them have already agreed to for two rounds running, and nothing about it introduces a new type or contradicts an existing one — so I'm treating it as adopted rather than blocking on a fourth round over something nobody has any actual grounds to contest.

There's one small thing left that neither of them noticed: in the process of dropping the Relay-prefix, they didn't fully agree on two leftover infrastructure names — Codex kept `RelayError` and named the client protocol `RequestAPIClient`; Claude renamed the error type to `AppError` but reverted the client protocol to `PulseRelayAPIClient`. That's not a real disagreement, just a name each of them didn't finish updating consistently with their own stated rule. I'm picking `AppError` (matches the "drop Relay branding from generic infra types" logic both of them were actually applying) and `RequestAPIClient` (what both of them used in round 2, and what Codex kept in round 3) — same kind of harmless tie-break the coordinator made on hex values back in design_handoff, not a new open item.

CONSENSUS: YES

## Final Output

**Architecture**, unchanged and now fully specified: server-authoritative REST (`/api/v1`) over PostgreSQL, an actor-based `RequestSyncCoordinator` as the sole mutator of request state, `AppSession` driving `AppGate`'s three-way routing, SwiftData as a disposable board/request cache plus a durable offline outbox, Keychain (`AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`) for session storage, zero third-party dependencies, push as wake-up-only.

**Module layout:** `App/` (entry, `AppSession`, `AppGate`), `Domain/` (models, events, reducer), `State/` (`RequestSyncCoordinator` + reducer tests), `Network/` (`RequestAPIClient`, endpoint/mapper code), `Persistence/` (SwiftData models, cache reset/recovery), `Notifications/` (push service, deep-link parsing), `Features/` (AuthGate, PodOnboarding, RelayBoard, RequestComposer, RequestDetail, Receipt, Profile, PodSettings), `Shared/` (Theme, timers, formatters, haptics, accessibility helpers).

**Data model, canonical naming:** `User`, `Pod`, `JoinCodeStatus`, `PodMembership`, `Request` (with `status: RequestStatus` staying at exactly 5 values — open/claimed/reopened/withdrawn/completed — plus a separate `closeReason: RequestCloseReason?` carrying `autoExpired`/`requesterWithdrawn`/`systemHousekeeping` so system-driven expiry and requester-driven withdrawal share one status but render different, honest copy off the same locked 11-state client card machine), `ActionType` (post/accept/release/withdraw/complete/**reBroadcast**), `ActionConflictCode`, `ActionOutcome`, `RequestAction` (a standalone, always-written audit-log table — one row per action attempt regardless of outcome, never owned by or nested inside a receipt), `ActionResult`, `Receipt` (a derived read-time view, constructible only once a `complete` action exists).

**API contract:** `GET /api/v1/health` (required first client call, gates everything else on reachability/contract version), `POST /api/v1/auth/apple`, `POST /api/v1/pods`, `POST /api/v1/pods/join` (hard 403 `already_in_pod` single-pod v1 cap), `POST /api/v1/pods/{id}/join-code/rotate`, `GET /api/v1/pods/{id}/state` (requests pre-sorted by a single BIGSERIAL-backed `displayOrder` column, no compound tie-break, no client re-sort), `POST /api/v1/requests`, `GET /api/v1/requests/{id}`, `POST /api/v1/requests/{id}/actions` (CAS via `UPDATE ... WHERE request_revision = $expected AND status = ANY($allowedFromStatuses) RETURNING *`; `expectedRequestRevision` is now required, non-optional, end to end — outbox to coordinator to wire), `GET /api/v1/requests/{id}/receipt`, `POST /api/v1/devices/apns-token`, `DELETE /api/v1/account` (audit/receipt rows survive, deleted party renders as "Former member").

**Persistence:** SwiftData `RequestSnapshot`/pod cache is disposable, purge-and-refetch on schema mismatch; `OutboxAction` is durable across relaunch/upgrade, with `expectedRequestRevision` optional only at that storage layer because the same model also queues brand-new `post` actions that have no prior revision to guard.

**Testing, three required tiers:** backend-only HTTP concurrency tests (accept-vs-accept, accept-vs-withdraw, deterministic conflict), a new local coordinator-concurrency tier (two real `RequestSyncCoordinator` instances racing an `accept` via `TaskGroup` against one shared test backend, asserting the winner/loser split lands correctly in each actor's own event stream), and the manual two-phone side-by-side demo — plus reducer unit tests that specifically prove a queued action rejected with a real conflict/forbidden/unauthorized outcome goes terminal and stops retrying, while only network/timeout failures retry.

## Final Output

**Architecture**, unchanged and now fully specified: server-authoritative REST (`/api/v1`) over PostgreSQL, an actor-based `RequestSyncCoordinator` as the sole mutator of request state, `AppSession` driving `AppGate`'s three-way routing, SwiftData as a disposable board/request cache plus a durable offline outbox, Keychain (`AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`) for session storage, zero third-party dependencies, push as wake-up-only.

**Module layout:** `App/` (entry, `AppSession`, `AppGate`), `Domain/` (models, events, reducer), `State/` (`RequestSyncCoordinator` + reducer tests), `Network/` (`RequestAPIClient`, endpoint/mapper code), `Persistence/` (SwiftData models, cache reset/recovery), `Notifications/` (push service, deep-link parsing), `Features/` (AuthGate, PodOnboarding, RelayBoard, RequestComposer, RequestDetail, Receipt, Profile, PodSettings), `Shared/` (Theme, timers, formatters, haptics, accessibility helpers).

**Data model, canonical naming:** `User`, `Pod`, `JoinCodeStatus`, `PodMembership`, `Request` (with `status: RequestStatus` staying at exactly 5 values — open/claimed/reopened/withdrawn/completed — plus a separate `closeReason: RequestCloseReason?` carrying `autoExpired`/`requesterWithdrawn`/`systemHousekeeping` so system-driven expiry and requester-driven withdrawal share one status but render different, honest copy off the same locked 11-state client card machine), `ActionType` (post/accept/release/withdraw/complete/**reBroadcast**), `ActionConflictCode`, `ActionOutcome`, `RequestAction` (a standalone, always-written audit-log table — one row per action attempt regardless of outcome, never owned by or nested inside a receipt), `ActionResult`, `Receipt` (a derived read-time view, constructible only once a `complete` action exists).

**API contract:** `GET /api/v1/health` (required first client call, gates everything else on reachability/contract version), `POST /api/v1/auth/apple`, `POST /api/v1/pods`, `POST /api/v1/pods/join` (hard 403 `already_in_pod` single-pod v1 cap), `POST /api/v1/pods/{id}/join-code/rotate`, `GET /api/v1/pods/{id}/state` (requests pre-sorted by a single BIGSERIAL-backed `displayOrder` column, no compound tie-break, no client re-sort), `POST /api/v1/requests`, `GET /api/v1/requests/{id}`, `POST /api/v1/requests/{id}/actions` (CAS via `UPDATE ... WHERE request_revision = $expected AND status = ANY($allowedFromStatuses) RETURNING *`; `expectedRequestRevision` is now required, non-optional, end to end — outbox to coordinator to wire), `GET /api/v1/requests/{id}/receipt`, `POST /api/v1/devices/apns-token`, `DELETE /api/v1/account` (audit/receipt rows survive, deleted party renders as "Former member").

**Persistence:** SwiftData `RequestSnapshot`/pod cache is disposable, purge-and-refetch on schema mismatch; `OutboxAction` is durable across relaunch/upgrade, with `expectedRequestRevision` optional only at that storage layer because the same model also queues brand-new `post` actions that have no prior revision to guard.

**Testing, three required tiers:** backend-only HTTP concurrency tests (accept-vs-accept, accept-vs-withdraw, deterministic conflict), a new local coordinator-concurrency tier (two real `RequestSyncCoordinator` instances racing an `accept` via `TaskGroup` against one shared test backend, asserting the winner/loser split lands correctly in each actor's own event stream), and the manual two-phone side-by-side demo — plus reducer unit tests that specifically prove a queued action rejected with a real conflict/forbidden/unauthorized outcome goes terminal and stops retrying, while only network/timeout failures retry.

===== THIS PHASE'S DISCUSSION SO FAR =====

**Codex (Delivery Lead · Visionary) — Round 1**

The strongest direction is to treat `pulse-relay` as a concurrency-and-trust correctness problem first, then as a UI product. That means the first deliverable is not a polished screen, but a provable state machine and backend arbitration path where two real users can race actions and always get exactly one winner with immediate, honest follow-up states.

Milestones:
- M1 (Day 1): Foundation lock and work breakdown. Freeze module ownership and contracts in shared implementation notes, create repo target map (`App`, `Domain`, `State`, `Network`, `Persistence`, `Notifications`, `Features`, `Shared`), and set up basic test targets. Exit gate: no unresolved naming/API type mismatches from tech specs.
- M2 (Days 1–2): Backend schema and migration baseline. Implement PostgreSQL schema, auth, pod create/join (including 403 `already_in_pod`), request lifecycle actions, `RequestAction` audit table, and `GET /api/v1/health` gate endpoint. Exit gate: seed script, OpenAPI-like contract artifacts, and one local DB test container boot.
- M3 (Days 2–4): Backend action CAS correctness and expiry policy. Implement `POST /requests/{id}/actions` with required `expectedRequestRevision` and allowed state transitions, including `reBroadcast` and `withdraw`/`release` exclusivity. Add server-side auto-expiry setting `withdrawn + autoExpired`. Exit gate: deterministic backend-only concurrency tests for accept-vs-accept and accept-vs-withdraw.
- M4 (Days 3–5, overlaps with M3): iOS domain and coordinator core. Implement canonical models/enums, `RequestCardPhase` reducer, `RequestSyncCoordinator` actor, outbox durability, `AppSession` bootstrap with health gate (`GET /health` first), and state banners. Exit gate: reducer unit tests and coordinator-level race tests added.
- M5 (Days 4–6): Core UI build of mandatory relay loop. Implement `AuthGate`, `PodOnboarding`, `RelayBoard`, `RequestComposer`, `RequestDetail`, and receipt view with Theme token-only styling and all required empty/loading/error/success states. Exit gate: no placeholder/blank states and no inline fonts/colors; loser transition visually handled as designed.
- M6 (Days 6–7): Push/deep-link and offline hardening. Implement APNs token registration, push as wake-up only (no payload trust), deep-link refetch, stale deep-link handling, and terminal-visibility gating rules. Exit gate: no UI state sourced from push payload.
- M7 (Days 7–8): End-to-end integration and demo hardening. Orchestrate two-device seeded-demo flow, verify side-by-side accept race and reopen/rebroadcast/withdraw paths, tune banner copy around real delivery uncertainty, and close remaining acceptance criteria.
- M8 (Days 8–9): Stabilization and packaging. Fix failing edge cases from the demo, run full verification suite, capture evidence artifacts, and prepare runbook for verification.

Dependencies:
- Health/reachability gate must be in place before any backend-dependent state is trusted in client UI.
- Backend CAS endpoint is blocking for any `RequestSyncCoordinator` action path.
- `RequestCardPhase` reducer and event contracts block UI binding; no view may model independent state flags.
- Push wake-up contract blocks all deep-linking and stale-link handling.
- Theme tokens and visual state machine block final acceptance review and visual QA.
- Acceptance test suite blocks handoff to next lane.

Risk mitigations:
- Biggest objection is overbuilding motion/accessory polish before the two-device arbitration proof. Mitigation: freeze a hard non-negotiable order where CAS correctness and no-optimistic outcomes are locked before any non-core visuals.
- APNs best-effort delivery creates user-visible uncertainty. Mitigation: server dispatch timing telemetry + explicit “uncertain delivery” banner when only push uncertainty exists.
- Offline replay loops can mask false states. Mitigation: explicit terminalization of conflict/forbidden/unauthorized queued actions; only network/timeout errors retry.
- Cache/schema drift can mask stale confidence. Mitigation: purge-and-refetch strategy with stale cache UI only, terminal confidence only after fresh sync.
- Backend reachability can fail in early validation. Mitigation: bootstrap refusal path with clear recovery/copy, no feature-specific data shown until `/health` and `canOperate` pass.

Verification plan:
- Continuous by milestone: unit tests for reducer, mapper/serialization, outbox state transitions, coordinator tests after each reducer shape change.
- Mandatory fixed gate 1: backend-only concurrent HTTP race tests for deterministic CAS outcomes.
- Mandatory fixed gate 2: coordinator concurrency test with two actors racing accept via shared backend and asserting event-stream winner/loser resolution.
- Mandatory fixed gate 3: physical two-device side-by-side incident demo covering post, race, release/reopen, still-open escalation, complete, and force-quit reconcilation.
- Final acceptance gate: no unauthenticated success states, health gate mandatory, 11-phase card machine behavior covered, and all core screens with defined empty/loading/success/error states in light and dark mode.

**Claude (Backend / Systems Engineer · Skeptic) — Round 1**

Let me stress-test the plan from the backend/systems side before we lock milestones, because I think there are at least two load-bearing gaps that six phases of very careful spec work have not actually closed.

First, sequencing. Everything downstream — the health-gate call, the CAS accept-race, the audit log, the receipt — is meaningless until there is a real Postgres instance running somewhere on the public internet with a real domain/IP the iOS client (and a second physical device) can reach. That has to be milestone zero, full stop, before a single SwiftUI screen gets built past AppGate. And I don't think we've actually pinned two things that are prerequisites to writing that milestone: what language/framework the backend is written in, and where it's hosted. Every phase so far has said "custom REST API over PostgreSQL" and left the implementation stack unstated. That's fine for an architecture doc but it's not fine for a project plan — you can't sequence build lanes for a backend nobody has picked a language for. I'd lock something boring and fast to stand up (a small Node/TypeScript or Go service is going to get us to a working `/health` endpoint faster than standing up Vapor with its own toolchain quirks, and neither choice is precluded by anything already decided since the "Apple-frameworks-only, no third-party deps" rule was scoped to the iOS client, not the server). Milestone zero's deliverable isn't "backend architecture designed" — it's "curl https://<real-host>/api/v1/health returns 200 from a machine that isn't localhost," because that's the actual test of DEC-prompt_contract-008 and DEC-tech_specs-006, and it's the one thing this whole six-phase spec has asserted as a requirement without ever being forced to prove it's achievable in this environment.

Second, and this is the one I actually want to raise as an objection rather than a housekeeping note: the acceptance bar locked back in next_steps_small is a literal two-phone side-by-side demo with real APNs-delivered push, and I don't think anyone has stress-tested whether that's achievable in whatever environment this gets built in. Real remote push notifications do not work on the iOS Simulator delivered from an actual backend — a simulator can only receive a push if you manually shove a payload at it via `xcrun simctl push`, which proves nothing about the server's real APNs integration. Getting genuine device-delivered push requires: an enrolled Apple Developer Program membership, an App ID with the Push Notifications capability turned on, a provisioning profile built against that capability, and a real APNs auth key (.p8) wired into the backend's push-sending code — plus two actual physical iPhones signed into two actual Apple IDs to run the demo on. If none of that exists yet in this build's environment, the plan as currently scoped has an acceptance criterion it structurally cannot meet, and nobody should discover that at the final review. I want the project plan to name this explicitly as the top delivery risk, with a fallback tier that's honest about what's actually provable without hardware/credentials: the backend concurrency test and the local coordinator-concurrency test (both already locked in tech_specs) can run and pass on CI/simulator alone with zero Apple push infrastructure, and those two tiers should be treated as the load-bearing proof that CAS arbitration works; the physical two-phone demo should be gated as "run if devices and a paid developer account are actually available in this environment," not silently assumed away or silently faked with `simctl push` and reported as if it were the real thing.

On the data side, I want the plan to include an explicit migration/seed milestone as its own line item, not folded into "backend endpoints implementation": a versioned, re-runnable SQL migration set (plain numbered .sql files applied in order is enough, no migration framework needed) covering all nine tables/enums locked in tech_specs, plus a seed script that creates exactly two real user accounts in one real pod — because [REDACTED:high_entropy] and DEC-next_steps_small-004 both depend on two real seeded accounts existing, and if that seeding is ad hoc/manual every time someone wants to test, the race-condition demo will quietly stop being run. I'd sequence it: schema + migrations + health endpoint + deploy → auth (Sign in with Apple token verification server-side) → pod endpoints (create/join/rotate, enforcing the single-pod cap) → request endpoints (post/fetch) → the actions endpoint with the CAS UPDATE and RequestAction audit write → backend HTTP concurrency test (this is the first real go/no-go gate, and it should block client work from being trusted, not just be "nice to have passing eventually") → APNs dispatch wiring behind its own flag so its absence doesn't block the rest → receipt endpoint → account deletion with placeholder-rendering. Client work can start in parallel on auth/onboarding screens against a mocked API client once the interface contract is fixed (it already is, from tech_specs), but no client screen that depends on real request state should be marked "working" until it's actually talking to the deployed backend, not a local stub — I've seen enough of this fleet's own visual-QA failures (blank screens, placeholder text reported as done) to not trust a screen that "looks right" against fake data.

Last thing: the plan needs verification and repair time budgeted as its own milestone, not implied. Concretely: after the three test tiers pass, there should be a dedicated pass for the things this fleet has actually broken before — dark mode on every core screen, no hardcoded font/color literals outside Theme.swift (two prior recorded incidents, per the anti-patterns list), and no screen shipped with placeholder/blank content. That should be scheduled as its own step with time reserved to actually fix what it finds, not assumed to fall out of "the screens were built to spec."

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Here's where round 1 landed: Codex laid out a full eight-milestone delivery plan (foundation lock → backend schema/migrations → CAS action endpoint → iOS coordinator/reducer → core UI → push/deep-link → two-device integration → stabilization), with dependencies, risk mitigations, and a three-tier verification plan built directly on what tech_specs already locked. That's a solid skeleton and nobody's pushing back on its overall shape.

But Claude, playing skeptic this round, poked three real holes in it that Codex's plan doesn't yet address:

1. **The backend has no chosen language or hosting target.** Every prior phase said "custom REST over PostgreSQL" as architecture, but nobody's actually picked what it's written in or where it runs — and you can't sequence a real milestone-zero without that. Claude wants "curl a real deployed `/health` endpoint from a non-localhost machine" as the literal first deliverable, not "backend architecture designed."
2. **The two-phone real-APNs demo may not be achievable in this build environment at all.** Simulators can't receive genuine server-sent push (only fake `simctl push` injection), and real device push needs a paid Apple Developer account, a provisioning profile with Push capability, a real `.p8` APNs key, and two physical iPhones on two Apple IDs. Claude wants this named explicitly as the top delivery risk with a fallback: treat the backend concurrency test + the local coordinator-concurrency test (both already locked, both provable on CI/simulator alone) as the load-bearing proof of CAS correctness, and gate the physical demo as "run only if hardware/credentials are actually available here" rather than silently assuming it'll happen or faking it and reporting it as real.
3. **Migration/seeding and verification/repair need to be their own explicit milestones**, not folded into vague "implement endpoints" or "polish" buckets — specifically a versioned SQL migration set plus a seed script producing two real accounts in one real pod (since the whole acceptance protocol depends on that existing reliably), and a dedicated dark-mode/no-hardcoded-literal/no-placeholder-screen pass with time actually reserved to fix what it finds, given this fleet's own recorded history of exactly those failures.

Codex hasn't had a chance to respond to any of this yet, so there's real open disagreement/addition here, not just phrasing to polish. Next round needs Codex to either fold these into the milestone plan (pick a concrete backend stack + host, add explicit migration/seed and verification/repair milestones, and re-tier the acceptance criteria around what's actually provable without hardware) or make a counter-case for why not.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round should settle: (1) a concrete backend language + hosting choice as milestone zero, (2) whether the physical two-device APNs demo is actually achievable in this environment and, if uncertain, how the acceptance bar gets honestly re-tiered, (3) explicit migration/seed and verification/repair milestones folded into the plan.

Global app-build rules:

- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.

----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.
